summary: Round 3, delta only. All three claimed kills re-measured in my own tree and all three are real, and they fail for the right reason. (1) The T1 fix: `keyFor(hop.from())` for `hop.from() - 1` and `checkpoint.sequence() + 1` for `checkpoint.sequence()` each now fail `theDELTASAfterTheCheckpointAreReplayed`, and each fails on the SECOND assertion (streamOfTerm(1) expected 1, was 0) with the first still green -- so the second assertion is not decoration, it is the only thing in that test that sees a first-uncovered-delta off-by-one. (2) The T7 fix: deleting the `crossFromCheckpoint` probe from the `neverOpened` branch now fails `aRunOfBURNEDEpochsStillStopsAtTheCheckpointBehindThem` (expected 500, was 4). (3) The fixture consolidation is inert -- the moved helpers are byte-identical to the deleted private copies, `TestClock` is still constructed fresh per `manager()` call so no state is shared across tests, and no cost number moves. Rules 4-5 hold across the delta: the one changed assertion (12 -> 11) tracks a changed fixture and is accompanied by a strictly stronger new assertion, not a loosening. ONE MINOR REMAINS AND IT IS THE SHAPE T7 WAS ABOUT: the sentinel-checkpoint fixture pins that the checkpoint was READ AND USED, not that the walk STOPPED, and a probe-without-break mutant on that branch survives all 298 tests -- measured. The sibling CONTINUE branch is pinned against exactly that mutant by a request count, so the asymmetry is visible in the tree. Nothing blocks.

findings.title: aRunOfBURNEDEpochsStillStopsAtTheCheckpointBehindThem pins that the checkpoint was USED, not that the walk STOPPED -- and the walk stopping is what the test is named for
findings.detail:
The fixture itself is LEGITIMATE, and I do not think it is dishonest. A checkpoint whose offsets disagree with its own chain's deltas is not a state production can reach -- `CheckpointWriter` snapshots `log.offsets()` -- but the fixture is not asserting anything about checkpoint fidelity. It is a discriminator: with an honest checkpoint the two code paths produce the same number, so the test would be vacuous, which is precisely what the author measured and says in the comment. Seeding an impossible value to make two paths observably different is a standard and sound technique, and it is not a weakening of anything.

What it proves is NARROWER than the probe's purpose. The probe exists to terminate the walk; the row's own headline is 'STOP WALKING, NOT READ FEWER DELTAS'. An offset assertion can only see whether the checkpoint's offsets entered the result. The asymmetry is visible inside this commit: the identical probe on the CONTINUE branch (ChainReplay.java:162) IS pinned against the same mutant -- I removed its `break` and `aPredecessorTOOSHORTToCheckpointStillStopsAtItsAncestorsCheckpoint` failed, because that test asserts `counts().total()`. The burned-epoch branch got a sentinel where its sibling got a request count.

BETTER FIXTURE, and it needs no impossible checkpoint: build epoch 1 with a long chain (say 60 deltas, K=1 so it checkpoints throughout), burn epoch 2, open epoch 3, and recover epoch 3 through a `CountingBinStore`, asserting `counts().total()` is a small constant. That kills the deletion mutant AND the probe-without-break mutant, and it uses only states production can reach. If both properties are wanted, keep the sentinel assertion for 'used' and add the count for 'stopped'.

WHY MINOR AND NOT MAJOR: the branch is unreachable in production today -- `ChainReplay.neverOpened`'s own javadoc records that `LocalSequencer.start` resolves burned epochs through `firstInheritableAncestor` first -- so the surviving mutant costs requests on a path no deployment reaches, and the correctness half of that branch IS pinned. The test is not empty: it kills probe deletion outright. This is a recorded-not-fixed candidate for the commit body or a backlog row, in the same spirit as T9.
findings.failure_scenario: A future session touching ChainReplay's burned-epoch branch -- M4.23 is the named candidate, since it owns the empty-prevEpoch gap in exactly this code -- refactors the probe so that it folds the checkpoint's offsets but no longer terminates the walk. The suite stays green (measured: 298 tests, 0 failures), every offset assertion still passes, and the takeover across a run of burned epochs silently goes back to O(all commit-log entries ever written) -- the exact regression this task exists to remove. Nothing in the tree fails, and the test whose NAME says 'STILL STOPS' is the test that passes.

findings.title: The T8 fix's 'dead imports are gone' is not true of this file -- fifteen remain
findings.surviving_mutation: n/a -- cosmetic, no behaviour is unconstrained by it. Recorded because it is a claim made to review that does not hold in the staged bytes, and this repository's own baselines record that pattern as the thing worth catching.
findings.detail: After the helper block was deleted, BinStore, Body, Checkpoint, Checkpoint.StreamOffsets, RunKey, IOException, Clock, Duration, Instant, ZoneId, ZoneOffset, LinkedHashMap, Map, UUID and CountDownLatch are each referenced exactly once in the file -- on their own import line. Verified by grep in my tree; the build is green because no check flags unused imports. The private copies, the second `noRenew()` and the orphan javadoc ARE gone as claimed; only the import half of T8 was not done. Also cosmetic: three runs of stray blank lines left by the deletions at lines 106-108 and 151-154.
findings.failure_scenario: A later reader of LocalSequencerBoundedRecoveryTest sees imports of Checkpoint, StreamOffsets, Body and CountingBinStore and believes the file contains checkpoint-seeding and body-writing fixtures that it does not; or a future edit re-adds a private helper shadowing a static import because the import list suggested the file already stood alone. No test is weakened, but the round-2 claim that the dead imports were removed does not hold in the staged bytes.
